item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Die britische Großbank Barclays (BARC.L) hat trotz eines Gewinnanstiegs den Abbau von rund 5000 Stellen angekündigt. Das Unternehmen setze auf Technologien wie Künstliche Intelligenz (KI), um Fixkosten zu senken und die Gesamtrendite zu verbessern, teilte das Institut am Donnerstag mit. Finanzchefin (CFO) Anna Cross erklärte, rund 60 Prozent des geplanten Stellenabbaus entfielen auf unterstützende Funktionen, etwa im Bereich der Softwareentwicklung. Dies sei eines der bisher deutlichsten Signale einer Großbank dafür, wie KI es Unternehmen ermögliche, die Mitarbeiterzahl in solchen Bereichen zu verringern. 1000 Stellen seien bereits weggefallen, der Rest solle bis Jahresende abgebaut werden, so Cross. Im dritten Quartal verbuchte die Bank einen Anstieg des Vorsteuergewinns um zwölf Prozent auf 2,3 Milliarden Pfund. Dies erlaube einen neuen Aktienrückkauf im Umfang von 500 Millionen Pfund. Bankchef C. S. Venkatakrishnan erklärte, er sei mit der anhaltenden operativen und finanziellen Dynamik zufrieden. Die Anleger zeigten sich jedoch nicht überzeugt: Die Aktie gab im frühen Handel um 2,5 Prozent nach. Die Ergebnisse zeichneten ein gemischtes Bild, insbesondere im Investmentbanking. Während die Erträge im Aktienhandel um 47 Prozent zulegten und damit die US-Konkurrenz übertrafen, brachen sie im Handel mit festverzinslichen Wertpapieren um 19 Prozent ein. Dies war ein stärkerer Rückgang als bei den US-Rivalen. "Ich bin enttäuscht, und Sie können sicher sein, dass dies meine volle Aufmerksamkeit erhalten wird", sagte Venkatakrishnan mit Blick auf diesen traditionell starken Bereich. Insgesamt verfehlte die Investmentbank-Sparte mit Erträgen von 3,1 Milliarden Pfund die Analystenschätzungen leicht.

item.title: Europe's STOXX 600 slips as mixed earnings and rising oil sour mood
item.description: Europe's STOXX 600 index fell nearly 1% on Thursday, surrendering all of the prior session's gains as investors weighed a slate of mixed earnings reports, while higher oil prices and rising French bond yields further dampened risk appetite.
item.dc:creator: Avinash P
item.content:encoded: Europe's STOXX 600 index fell nearly 1% on Thursday, surrendering all of the prior session's gains as investors weighed a slate of mixed earnings reports, while higher oil prices and rising French bond yields further dampened risk appetite. The pan-European STOXX 600 (.STOXX) was down 0.95% at 638.38 points by 0855 GMT, after gaining over 0.9% on Wednesday. "We have some big concerns in the market, one is the situation in the Middle East... So that is sending oil prices higher and the other one is obviously bond yields," said Joost Van Leenders, senior investment strategist at Van Lanschot Kempen Investment. "You have those risk factors and the positive factors which vary from day to day....and make for a bit of volatility in the markets," he said. Oil prices climbed more than 2% after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia [USN:L1N46801N TEXT:"stoked concerns about broader escalation"] and supply disruption. Energy-dependent Europe has been hit by soaring energy costs, which have stoked price pressures and weighed on the broader index. Additionally, the yield spread between France's 10-year bond and German Bunds also hit a fresh 15-year high amid political uncertainty and protests in France. Kicking off European bank earnings, Barclays (BARC.L) shares erased earlier losses to trade flat after the company [USN:L6N4680EP TEXT:"reported a third-quarter"] profit miss. The lender separately said it would cut around 5,000 jobs, or 5% of its workforce this year. Despite this, the banking index (.SX7E) fell 2.7%. Hermes (HRMS.PA) fell 7.3% after the Birkin bag maker posted [USN:L6N4680E3 TEXT:"slightly weaker-than-expected"] quarterly revenue, with the drop weighing on the luxury index (.STXLUXP) . Nestle (NESN.S) added 1.2% after reporting better-than-expected [USN:L6N4680BP TEXT:"organic sales growth"] for the third quarter. The food and beverage index (.SX3P) gained 0.6%, one of the few sectors trading higher. The tech index (.SX8P) came under renewed pressure, tracking a global selloff, and was down 2.1%. AI-related shares such as Infineon (IFXGn.DE) , STMicroelectronics (STMPA.PA) and ASML (ASML.AS) fell between 2.8% and 3.6%. [USN:L8N46807V TEXT:"BE Semiconductor Industries"] (BESI.AS) and [USN:L6N4671BR TEXT:"SAP"] (SAPG.DE) fell 3.1% and 1%, respectively, after their quarterly earnings. Solid earnings from Meta Platforms (META.O) on Wednesday were not enough to placate investor worries about the sustainability and profitability of massive AI spending, reviving concerns that have triggered several selloffs in AI stocks this year. Among other stocks, UCB (UCB.BR) gained 12.2% after biopharmaceutical group [USN:L6N4680D9 TEXT:"upgraded its 2026 guidance"] on strong demand for its Bimzelx and Cimzia drugs.

item.title: Westpac's latest job cuts not AI-driven, spokesperson says
item.description: About 140 roles affected by workforce changes at Australian lender Westpac this week were part of a broader organisational restructure, not AI-driven job cuts, a spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Anjali Singh, Kumar Tanishk
item.content:encoded: About 140 roles affected by workforce changes at Australian lender Westpac (WBC.AX) this week were part of a broader organisational restructure, not AI-driven job cuts, a spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday. The Finance Sector Union, which represents bank and finance workers in the country said in a separate statement earlier in the day that Westpac had joined larger rival National Australia Bank (NAB.AX) in accelerating the rollout of "job-destroying AI". The spokesperson said Westpac notified the FSU of the changes on Monday, a day before NAB announced plans to cut up to [USN:L4N4651N3 TEXT:"2,500 jobs"] as part of efforts to simplify operations and reduce costs Australia's banking industry has undergone [USN:L3N3UV1F1 TEXT:"significant workforce"] changes in recent years as lenders streamline operations and rein in costs The changes come against the backdrop of a softening labour market, with Australia's jobless rate [USN:AZN4TP17R TEXT:"rising to 4.7%"] in September after a prolonged period of high interest rates "These changes are not related to AI but rather a broader organisational restructure that's been underway for some time," the spokesperson said on Thursday The changes are likely to be down to "duplication cuts in risk, institutional and finance, not roles displaced by a model," said Hersh Oberoi, global research director at Balfour Capital Group The FSU added that more than 10,000 banking jobs had been lost over the past two years and warned that further cuts could add pressure on workers already carrying heavier workloads "A lack of strong regulatory guardrails for AI is another factor adding to workers' sense of vulnerability," the union added Oberoi said AI is likely to have a limited effect on jobs in the Australian banking industry over the next six months but a substantial one over three to five years, with the first impact seen by contractors and consultants Westpac shares ended 0.4% higher at A$35.68. The stock is down about 7.6% year to date

item.title: Love affair to staged arrest: how a Romanian from England was jailed in Russia as a spy
item.description: Springtime in a park. Grey sky. A young man in a blue knitted hat and Adidas backpack walks down a path. Two burly security agents spring from a van and pin him to the pavement.
item.dc:creator: Mark Trevelyan
item.content:encoded: Springtime in a park. Grey sky. A young man in a blue knitted hat and Adidas backpack walks down a path. Two burly security agents spring from a van and pin him to the pavement. "What is your name?" asks a voice in English as a gloved hand holds the man's face towards the camera. "David Adrian Kercso," he swiftly responds. Where is he from? "Romania. Romania." The video, released by Russia's FSB security service and published by state media, purports to show the arrest of Kercso, now 23, a Romanian citizen who grew up in England and was sentenced earlier this year to 15 years for spying for Ukraine. Reuters has not been able to verify all of the evidence in Kercso's case. But what is clear is that the arrest video is not what it purports to be: Reuters analysis of the video and of court records of his detention shows that at the time it was made he had already been in Russian custody for months. It was filmed in a park inside Russia, in the southern city of Sochi. But Kercso's arrest was first announced elsewhere, by pro-Russian separatists across the border in Abkhazia, a breakaway region of neighbouring Georgia, who released their own video of him in their custody the day before he first turned up in a Russian court. The FSB did not respond to requests for comment for this story, including why it would release a video depicting the purported arrest of a suspect who was already in custody. Requests for comment were also sent to the Abkhazian separatists' SGB security agency, the Russian embassy in London, the Romanian and Ukrainian foreign ministries. None replied. To Kercso's family, who say he was lured to the Black Sea coast to pursue a romance with a woman he had met online, the FSB video of a staged arrest is just another bizarre turn in a story that alarmed them from the outset. He hopes to lodge an appeal against his conviction. "I told him to not go there because it's very dangerous, because it's a war," his mother Julia Kercso told Reuters. "And he never listened to me yet." MOTHER WARNED HIM NOT TO GO In late 2023, Kercso was living in the English city of Reading, west of London, working for a company that recycles electronics, when he first connected online with a woman called Valeria. She was from Abkhazia, a picturesque sliver of Georgia's mountainous Black Sea coast that has been in the hands of separatists since the early 1990s. An online romance blossomed, and his family says he travelled via Turkey in August 2024 to meet her. Reuters obtained contact information for Valeria from the family but did not receive a reply to requests sent to her for comment. According to Kercso's accounts to his family, the couple met up in Sochi, and after a few days crossed the border into Abkhazia, where Kercso stayed through the autumn. But his mother said the relationship deteriorated as he began to run short of money, and he told his family he would return home. His trip back was planned for November 28, 2024, but he never arrived. That day, he stopped answering phone calls and messages. In subsequent letters from prison, Kercso said that was the day he was arrested in Abkhazia. The first announcement of Kercso's arrest came two weeks later from the Abkhazian separatist authorities, who released a video on December 13 depicting their own SGB security service leading the young man from a car into a building. He was shown confessing that he had been in contact with Ukrainian intelligence and had been told to film Abkhazian military sites with a drone. In his letters, Kercso says that initial confession videotaped in Abkhazia had consisted of a text he had been ordered to memorise by his captors. The separatists told him that if he recited it on camera he would be sent home. But instead, he wrote, he was brought to the border and transferred into the custody of the Russian FSB. The day after the Abkhazians released their video, Kercso was indeed in Russian custody, appearing before a judge at Sochi's Khostinsky District Court on December 14, according to court records available online. It was the first of 10 court appearances that would be registered over the next four months, at which his detention in Russia would be extended roughly every two weeks. TAKEN FROM JAIL TO FILM 'ARREST' In his letters, Kercso says that the staged Russian video of his "arrest" was filmed in mid-April in Sochi, after he had already been captured in Abkhazia, transferred to Russia and held there for four months. He was awakened in jail around dawn by FSB officers who took him to a nearby location to film it. Reuters analysis of the video is consistent with this account. Though the exact date cannot be established, ample green foliage is clearly visible, showing it was filmed after the start of spring, and could not have been filmed before he began the four months of detention documented in his 10 Sochi court appearances since December. The location - a strip of parkland along Sochi's Matsesta River - can be established from visible features. These include the pathway layout, a bridge pillar, lamp posts, trees, a grassy strip and a wall, all of which match archive and satellite imagery of the area. Evgeny Smirnov, a Russian lawyer familiar with the case, said it was common for the FSB to compel suspects to film dramatic arrest scenes long after they are detained. "We have seen this in dozens of cases where individuals detained months earlier are taken to a city street, a forest, or a train station so that a staged arrest video can be filmed," he said. Kercso says in his letters that in the months following his transfer to Russia he was beaten, held in isolation and tortured. Reuters could not independently verify those allegations. When he was sentenced, the FSB said he had transmitted the location of Russian air-defence systems in Sochi to a Ukrainian intelligence agency in the summer of 2024. Video released by the agency showed him confessing to that charge. Kercso says that confession was also coerced. "None of that happened, they stole my life for no reason and fabricated everything," he wrote. He has learned Russian in prison, misses his family deeply and dreams of returning home. "Now I know that coming here was a huge mistake," he said. "I was blinded by love and didn't see the warning signs."

item.title: Israeli settlers steal Palestinians' olives as attacks on harvest grow more violent
item.description: Settlers have intimidated Palestinians harvesting their olives in the occupied West Bank for decades, but this year, not only has violence increased sharply, theft has been widespread.
item.dc:creator: Pesha Magid, Lina Obeid
item.content:encoded: Brought to tears as he recalled Israeli settlers hitting his cherished olive trees with sticks and taking off with the olives, Palestinian Ahmed Salem said he feared being attacked if he tried to intervene. Settlers have intimidated Palestinians harvesting their olives in the occupied West Bank for decades, but this year, not only has [USN:L8N4620II TEXT:"violence increased sharply"], theft has been widespread, according to Palestinians, Israeli rights groups and the UN. The settlers dumped Salem's olives into sacks and then drove them to a nearby Israeli settler outpost to be pressed into olive oil, the 50-year-old Palestinian told Reuters of the incident around two weeks ago near his village Lubban al-Gharbi. "How would you feel if something that belonged to you was being violated, and you could do nothing about it?" he asked. The couple living in the outpost, whose olive press settlers have urged Israelis to use for West Bank olives, declined multiple Reuters requests for comment, while the Yesha Council, which oversees Israeli settlements in the West Bank, did not immediately respond. The attacks have accelerated ahead of an Israeli election next week that opinion polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his pro-settler coalition could lose to opponents who have taken a [USN:L6N4660BW TEXT:"more critical stance"] against settler violence. 'SETTLERS CAN COME AND GO FREELY' The olive harvest starts with the onset of cooler weather, allowing Palestinian families to gather in the lush, terraced groves that they have groomed for generations. "My six-year-old son remembers going there with me, eating there, making tea there," Salem said. With the establishment of hundreds of small settler outposts under Netanyahu's government since 2022, the military has increasingly restricted Palestinian access to areas nearby, including many olive groves. "This creates a situation where Palestinians, in many of the cases, many of the lands, especially in proximity to settlements and outposts, cannot enter the land and harvest the trees," said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Israeli rights group Yesh Din. "But settlers can come and go freely, and that's what they do." Even when Palestinians can access their trees, it is not without risk. Yesh Din on Wednesday reported 125 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters over the 24 days since the season began and 168 incidents of crop theft, with Israeli military forces present in at least a quarter of cases. An Israeli military official said it takes [USN:L6N46304S TEXT:"acts of violence"], criminal activity and attempts to undermine security very seriously. The official did not refer to settlers or comment on the reports of olive theft in the presence of the Israeli military, which has separately [USN:L8N45F1FN TEXT:"uprooted trees with excavators"], citing what it said was a need to prevent Palestinian attacks. The removal of Palestinians' olives has met with widely differing responses from Israeli rabbis. "I call it theft. From my perspective, I define it as theft or robbery, and it is forbidden," said Zev Weitman, the rabbi for the Alon Shvut settlement south of Bethlehem. Prominent Orthodox rabbi Dov Lior said settlers should harvest across the West Bank, asserting in an open letter that Palestinians had no ownership rights to the land and that harvesting olives fulfilled "the commandment of conquering the land." 'IT'S EITHER US OR OUR ENEMY', SETTLERS SAY ON SOCIAL MEDIA Hundreds of acres of the land around Salem's village, Lubban al-Gharbi, including olive groves, were fenced off and seized between 2023 and 2026 by Avichai Farm, an Israeli settler outpost built on a nearby hill. Salem said villagers have seen settlers harvest olives from the seized land and take them to the outpost's olive press. At the start of the olive harvest, settlers posted on social media calling on Israelis to harvest West Bank olives and bring them to Avichai Farm's press. "Both fine oil and strengthening the Jewish hold on the vast expanses of our land!," read a message on a settler Telegram group. "It's either us or our enemy!" The press at Avichai Farm advertises "premium products produced by Avichai Farm" with olive oil at about $20 a bottle via a website run by the Farms Association, a settler group that Reuters has reported receives significant financial support from the Israeli government, which says the aim is to promote peace. The Farms Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment and the couple who live on the farm with their children declined to be interviewed by a Reuters reporter who approached the area on Sunday. On a road leading to Avichai Farm, Reuters spoke to a man who declined to be identified and said he had driven from a settlement around 90 minutes away to press 14 bags of olives from trees he said he grew himself. Lubban al-Gharbi villagers and other Palestinians who have lost land to settler expansion say the harvesting of olives from trees in groves seized from Palestinian land constitutes theft. UN bodies and most countries deem Israel's settlements on land occupied in war illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied. 'WE PAY IN BLOOD FOR THE OLIVES' During this year's olive harvest, Palestinian authorities say three Palestinians have been killed in daily militant settler attacks, which have also injured several journalists, [USN:L6N46304S TEXT:"European diplomats and a French mayor"]. Stahl from the Yesh Din Israeli rights group said the violence was "part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing, paving the way for the annexation of the West Bank without its Palestinian population." Israel, which has [USN:L1N3W407X TEXT:"considered the idea of annexation"], said it is investigating some of the incidents. An Israeli government spokesperson said olives "picked by a Jew in the ancestral homeland of the Jewish people" did not constitute theft and that Jews owned and cultivated "millions of olive trees" in the area. No one should take the law into their own hands, the spokesperson added. Palestinian farmer Samer Ben Shamsi said masked settlers attacked him on October 9 in the Palestinian village of Beita near Nablus, then sped away in a pickup truck with his harvest of olives after he and other farmers fled. "This year, they steal without fear because they have a state and a powerful force backing them," Ben Shamsi said, referring to the security forces. Within the past year alone, settlers had shot him in the leg, beaten him and smashed his possessions, he said. "We pay in blood for the olives."

item.title: Hermès-La croissance ralentit au T3, pénalisée par les accessoires en Chine
item.description: Hermès a publié jeudi un chiffre d'affaires du troisième trimestre légèrement inférieur aux attentes, les ventes de la division Vêtement et Accessoires du fabricant des sacs Birkin ayant reculé pour la première fois depuis plusieurs années en raison d'une faible demande sur son marché clé, la Chine.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Parodi, Tassilo Hummel, Elena Smirnova
item.content:encoded: Hermès (HRMS.PA) a publié jeudi un chiffre d'affaires du troisième trimestre légèrement inférieur aux attentes, les ventes de la division Vêtement et Accessoires du fabricant des sacs Birkin ayant reculé pour la première fois depuis plusieurs années en raison d'une faible demande sur son marché clé, la Chine. Ce résultat inférieur aux attentes, qui intervient peu après [USN:L8N45Y1DP TEXT:"des résultats trimestriels"] également inférieurs aux attentes pour LVMH (LVMH.PA) , pourrait renforcer les inquiétudes des investisseurs quant à la capacité d’Hermès à résister au ralentissement généralisé du secteur du luxe. Vers 09h45 GMT, à la Bourse de Paris, l'action reculait de 8,5% à 1.240 euros, lanterne rouge du CAC 40 (.CAC40) , après la publication d'une croissance trimestrielle de 4,3%, la plus faible enregistrée par le groupe depuis le début de l'année 2020, lorsque la pandémie l'avait contraint à fermer temporairement ses boutiques dans le monde. Lors d'une conférence téléphonique, le directeur financier d'Hermès, Éric du Halgouët, a déclaré aux journalistes que le marché chinois, crucial pour le groupe, restait "très difficile", tout en se disant confiant quant aux perspectives de long terme dans le pays et en confirmant la poursuite des investissements du groupe en Chine. Les ventes trimestrielles ont progressé de 4,3% sur un an à taux de change constants, à 4,10 milliards d'euros, contre une croissance de 5,2% attendue par les analystes interrogés par Visible Alpha. Les ventes de la division Maroquinerie-Sellerie, qui comprend les emblématiques sacs Birkin et Kelly, ont progressé de 10,8%, tandis que celles de l'activité Vêtement et Accessoires, qui représente plus d'un quart du chiffre d'affaires du groupe, ont reculé de 2% par rapport à l'an dernier. Eric du Halgouët a précisé que ce recul de Vêtement et Accessoires tenait exclusivement de la faiblesse de la demande chinoise pour les accessoires vendus en grands volumes, tandis que la division continuait de croître dans toutes les autres régions. Le prêt-à-porter seul a progressé sur le trimestre, y compris en Chine, a-t-il ajouté. OPTIMISME SUR L'ACTIVITÉ AUX ÉTATS-UNIS Les consommateurs chinois, qui représentent environ un cinquième des achats mondiaux de produits de luxe, ont longtemps constitué le principal moteur de croissance du secteur. La demande s'est toutefois nettement affaiblie depuis la pandémie de COVID-19. Éric du Halgouët a estimé que, à fin septembre, malgré un léger ralentissement au troisième trimestre, l'activité restait stable en Chine, ce qui constituait déjà une performance notable compte tenu des difficultés du marché. À l’inverse, le groupe s’est montré optimiste quant à l’évolution de son activité aux États-Unis, où il a récemment ouvert des boutiques dans des villes de taille intermédiaire, au-delà des grandes métropoles côtières. Selon Éric du Halgouët, la croissance a été portée par l’ensemble des magasins du pays et par toutes les catégories de produits. Interrogé sur [USN:L8N4650AN TEXT:"les violences"] qui ont éclaté en France ces derniers jours et qui ont conduit au pillage de l'un de ses magasins à Marseille, Hermès a indiqué renforcer ses mesures de sécurité. Le groupe a toutefois jugé prématuré d'évaluer l'impact potentiel de ces événements sur son activité et, surtout, sur le tourisme. La boutique de Marseille n'est pas près de rouvrir, a déclaré Éric du Halgouët aux analystes lors de la présentation des ventes du troisième trimestre, précisant que des vitrines avaient également été brisées dans les magasins de l'avenue George-V à Paris ainsi qu'à Nantes et Lyon, sans qu'aucune intrusion ne soit constatée dans ces points de vente. Selon plusieurs analystes, les investisseurs sont de plus en plus nombreux à considérer que la valorisation historiquement élevée d'Hermès, portée par une décennie de forte croissance, pourrait progressivement se rapprocher des niveaux observés dans le reste du secteur, à mesure que le rythme d'expansion du groupe ralentit. Plusieurs [USN:L8N4670PT TEXT:"revendeurs"] interrogés par Reuters estiment par ailleurs que la disponibilité accrue des sacs Birkin sur le marché de la seconde main a réduit une partie de leur attrait, suggérant que le modèle économique fondé sur la rareté pourrait être davantage mis à l'épreuve. L'attrait du Birkin reste toutefois "intact", a déclaré Éric du Halgouët, ajoutant que le groupe maintenait son objectif d'augmenter ses capacités de production et ses volumes d'environ 6% par an au cours des prochaines années.

item.title: Galderma lifts outlook for second quarter in a row after sales jump
item.description: Swiss skincare company Galderma raised its full-year sales guidance on Thursday for the second time in two quarters after strong demand for its therapeutic dermatology products drove robust growth in the first nine months of the year.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Swiss skincare company Galderma (GALD.S) raised its full-year sales guidance on Thursday for the second time in two quarters after strong demand for its therapeutic dermatology products drove robust growth in the first nine months of the year. The company reported net sales of $4.77 billion for January to September, up 25.1% from a year earlier. Third-quarter sales growth was 26%. Galderma raised its full-year net sales growth forecast to between 22.5% and 23.5% from 19% to 21%. Its shares rose as much as 5.8% in morning trade. The stock has more than tripled in value since the company listed on the Swiss stock exchange in March 2024. Injectable aesthetics sales rose 13.2% in the first nine months, while dermatological skincare sales increased 16.2%. Therapeutic dermatology sales jumped 64.4%, helped in part by strong demand for its Nemluvio product. CEO Flemming Ornskov said the company was assessing the impact of so-called Section 232 tariffs that took effect in the US in September, including on Nemluvio. With companies facing higher costs from disruptions linked to the US-Iran conflict, pricing is under close scrutiny across the industry. Ornskov noted that competitors in markets such as China and India operated from a lower cost base. "But given that we are segmented more to premium, we're holding up really well," he said.

item.title: Barclays to slash 5,000 jobs in AI-powered cost-cutting drive
item.description: Barclays said it is cutting around 5,000 jobs or 5% of its workforce this year, as it uses technology such as AI to slash fixed costs and improve returns.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence White
item.content:encoded: Barclays (BARC.L) said it is cutting around 5,000 jobs or 5% of its workforce this year, as it uses technology such as AI to slash fixed costs and improve returns. The job cuts were revealed as Barclays reported third-quarter profit of £2.3 billion ($3.08 billion), up 12% from a year ago but undershooting analysts' forecasts as its fixed income trading business underperformed. "I am disappointed, and you can be sure this will get my attention," CEO C.S. Venkatakrishnan said about the bank's traditional strength of fixed income trading, blaming a volatile quarter and weak trading in rates and credit products in particular. The bank said it had taken a further £201 million in "structural cost actions" in the third quarter, part of its longer-term plan to reduce expenses like staff costs through greater use of technology. Around 60% of the overall job cuts will impact staff in support functions such as developers, CFO Anna Cross told reporters, in one of the clearest signs yet from a big bank of how AI is enabling firms to reduce headcount in such roles. Cross said 1,000 roles have already gone, with the remainder to be cut by the end of the year. "The cuts illustrate just how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years," said Will Howlett, financials analyst at fund management business Quilter Cheviot. [USN:L4N45Y1A9 TEXT:"Companies worldwide including tech giant Microsoft"] (MSFT.O) and HSBC have announced layoffs this year, as automation increasingly impacts employment. Barclays shares slipped 0.1%, outperforming other lenders (.SX7P) . The bank's shares have fallen 12% so far this year, in line with European peers which have sold off after years of rallying as higher interest rates lifted profits. Shore Capital said in a note that the results were weaker than expected due to the disappointing performance by the investment bank. BUDGET LOOMS Barclays is the first major European lender to report its quarterly earnings, with British banks' results likely to be overshadowed by finance minister John Healey's first budget on October 28, where further taxes on banks may be levied. Healey has refused to rule out hiking taxes on banks' bumper profits despite intensive public and private lobbying by the industry in recent months, as the finance minister mulls higher taxes to help fund the Labour government's policy agenda and as higher borrowing costs eat into the public purse. Banks have argued they are already highly taxed compared with other jurisdictions and that any such levy would curb lending. INVESTMENT BANK'S MIXED QUARTER Barclays' investment bank reported total income in the third quarter of £3.1 billion, lower than forecasts for £3.3 billion. Third-quarter earnings from Barclays' Wall Street rivals earlier this month showed the cyclical nature of investment bank revenue, as [USN:L4N4600TB TEXT:"dealmaking slowed and fixed income desks underperformed"], with only equities trading sustaining the strong momentum seen in the first half of the year. Barclays' equities revenue rose 47%, outperforming the average 37% gain across the top five US players according to a Reuters calculation from company statements. The British lender, however, saw income from fixed income trading slide 19% to £1 billion, weaker than a 5% drop among its US peers and worse than analysts' forecasts for £1.3 billion. ($1 = 0.7461 pounds)

item.title: Ozempic wave boosts US cobblers and tailors as Americans tighten their belts
item.description: Over the past year, leather repairers have seen a spike in requests for their services due to rapid weight loss — not just for belts, but also for shoe and bag strap adjustments tailored to customers' trimmer bodies.
item.dc:creator: Danielle Kaye, Alexander Marrow
item.content:encoded: Lorraine Scott has spent at least $300 to tailor her pants and jeans since losing 60 pounds on weight-loss drugs over the past year. This is the fourth story in a five-part Reuters series on how weight-loss drugs are changing the way people shop and eat, and how companies are responding to the trend. "Most of the things in my closet didn't fit anymore," she said. The 42-year-old Atlanta resident, who is known as Lorraine Kamesha to her YouTube followers, has opted to alter her favorite pairs of pants instead of investing in new ones as her weight fluctuates, while turning to fast fashion for the rest of her wardrobe. US consumers taking weight-loss drugs like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro have turned to cobblers and tailors as they try to save money while shedding pounds, motivated in part by a cost-of-living squeeze and rising out-of-pocket costs for the drugs as US employers [USN:L1N44L0V0 TEXT:"increasingly drop GLP-1 coverage"]. Over the past year, leather repairers have seen a spike in requests for their services due to rapid weight loss — not just for belts, but also for shoe and bag strap adjustments tailored to customers' trimmer bodies. The uptick in demand for alterations underscores how weight-loss drugs are upending the retail sector, with some corners of the industry well-positioned to benefit while others struggle to adapt. About 11% of US adults are on GLP-1 drugs to lose weight, according to Gallup, forcing millions of consumers to look for affordable ways to [USN:L6N43B0UY TEXT:"revamp their wardrobes"]. Cobblers Direct, an online shoe and handbag repair shop with 25 brick-and-mortar stores in Texas and a nationwide mail-in service, is seeing double-digit year-on-year growth in its belt-shortening business, said CEO Stephen Kelly. The company, whose around 100 artisans will soon be operating from a new, nearly 30,000-square-foot warehouse in Austin, is now shortening as much as 500 belts each week, Kelly said. Customers, he said, have been walking into the stores with five or six belts slung across their shoulder. After getting a few more holes punched in, some have asked to keep the extra flap of leather as a "badge of honor." "They'll pull their belt out and show how long their belt originally was. And then they tuck it back into their waistline," Kelly said. About 80% of GLP-1 users are living in clothes that no longer fit, waiting six months on average before buying anything new, according to a survey of more than 700 US adults using weight-loss drugs by telehealth platform Trimi. Jeans are the most disrupted article of clothing, the survey found, with 90% of users lamenting poor fit. After going off weight-loss drugs, people regain on average 60% of their lost weight within a year, researchers at the University of Cambridge found this year, adding to users' reluctance to go all-in on an entirely new wardrobe. At family-owned Jim's Cobbler Concierge in Manhattan, customers last year started bringing in belts by the dozens, said client relations director CJ Burgos — a trend so sweeping that the store has dubbed it "belt-zempic." GLP-1 users are even seeing their feet shrink, Burgos said, prompting an uptick in shoe adjustments. "It's helped the business, but we've also helped clients save," said Burgos, who has also brought in belts to shorten since losing about 60 pounds on Ozempic. SECONDHAND SEIZES THE MOMENT, TOO GLP-1 users are tightening their belts in more ways than one. The drugs' surging popularity in the US is also boosting discount chains, thrift shops and secondhand clothing platforms as many users refrain from splurging on new clothes while their size remains in flux. Compared to other business tailwinds, what sets GLP-1s apart is "the scale and speed," said Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at online thrift store ThredUp. Shoppers are shifting to smaller sizes, especially when buying jeans: 43% of buyers who started above a waist size 28 are now buying smaller jeans than when they joined ThredUp, Rotem said. Stitch Fix, an online personal styling service, is now offering more adjustable sizing and stretchy fabrics so that people who are rapidly losing weight have the "right apparel to help them bridge multiple sizes," said CEO Matt Baer. He estimated that at least 20% of the company's new clients are on a GLP-1 medication and looking for help finding new sizes. "We've always known that resale and thrift are very popular choices for people in life transition," said Rotem of ThredUp. "As we see that there are many more people in life transition with the advent of GLP-1s, we're leaning into that." item.title: Sainsbury's raises profit outlook but sales growth slowdown hits shares
item.description: Sainsbury's , Britain's second-biggest supermarket group, followed industry leader Tesco in upgrading the lower end of its full-year profit outlook on Thursday, but slower sales growth in its second quarter sent its shares down 4%.
item.dc:creator: James Davey
item.content:encoded: Sainsbury's (SBRY.L) , Britain's second-biggest supermarket group, followed industry leader Tesco in upgrading the lower end of its full-year profit outlook on Thursday, but slower sales growth in its second quarter sent its shares down 4%. Sainsbury's published its first-half results two weeks after media reports that it held [USN:L6N45R0PU TEXT:"merger talks"] with smaller rival Morrisons earlier this year but walked away. CEO Simon Roberts declined to comment on the reports. "What I can say is that we're completely focused on the opportunities ahead for Sainsbury's," he said on a call with reporters. Sainsbury's, which has a 15.2% [USN:L8N45V0XH TEXT:"share"] of Britain's grocery market, said like-for-like sales, excluding fuel, rose 1.2% in its second quarter to September 12, below analysts' average forecast of 1.9%, having been up 2.3% in the [USN:L8N43209G TEXT:"prev"][USN:L8N43209G TEXT:"ious quarter"]. Tesco's (TSCO.L) [USN:L8N45U08P TEXT:"second-quarter"] underlying sales were also softer. SHARES FALL Shares in Sainsbury's fell 4%, paring 2026 gains to 6.4%. Analysts pointed to concerns the softer sales growth could continue into the key Christmas quarter, while the supermarket group cautioned the market would remain "very competitive". "There is also no upgraded buyback announcement to support the stock, like we saw at Tesco’s H1 results," said analysts at Bernstein. Roberts said the summer trading partly reflected multiple heatwaves which changed shopping habits. He also said Sainsbury's was up against a strong comparative performance in the first half last year when like-for-like sales rose 4.5%, boosted by disruption at competitors Marks & Spencer (MKS.L) , the Co-op and Asda. The Middle East conflict and its impact on energy prices also ate into discretionary household expenditure during the first half of this year. "Given the strength of our performance in the previous summer, we're actually pretty encouraged by the performance we've seen," said Roberts. "We're going into Christmas with a strong plan and real momentum," he said, adding consumers were waiting to see the impact on them of the government's budget statement on October 28. In July, Sainsbury's agreed to [USN:L4N43X0ML TEXT:"sell"] its Argos general merchandise business to Swift Partners for £120 million ($161 million). For the first half, Sainsbury's posted continuing underlying operating profit of £525 million, up 3.6%, reflecting volume growth in food and cost savings. It now forecasts full-year to end-February 2027 underlying operating profit of between £1.025 billion and £1.065 billion, up from previous guidance, adjusted for the disposal of Argos, of £965 million to £1.065 billion. ($1 = 0.7461 pounds) (This story has been refiled to fix a typo in paragraph 2.)

item.title: Hermes revenue growth slows as Chinese consumers cut spending on accessories
item.description: Birkin bag maker Hermes posted softer third-quarter revenue growth than expected on Thursday as sales in its ready-to-wear and accessories division fell for the first time in years due to weak demand in key market China.
item.dc:creator: Tassilo Hummel, Alessandro Parodi
item.content:encoded: [USN:L6N46012F TEXT:"Birkin bag maker"] Hermes (HRMS.PA) posted softer third-quarter revenue growth than expected on Thursday as sales in its ready-to-wear and accessories division fell for the first time in years due to weak demand in key market China. Hermes' miss, which follows [USN:L6N45Y0VL TEXT:"LVMH's downbeat quarterly sales update"] earlier this month, looked likely to further unsettle investors about the company's resilience in the face of a wider luxury sector slowdown. Shares in the French brand slid 5% in early trade. Hermes finance chief Eric du Halgouet told journalists on a call that the Chinese market, Hermes' single-largest, was "very difficult", but added he remained confident about long-term prospects and would keep investing in the country. Quarterly sales rose 4.3% year-on-year in currency-adjusted terms to €4.10 billion ($4.6 billion), slightly below an expected growth rate of 5.2% from analysts polled by Visible Alpha. The results marked Hermes' weakest quarterly sales growth rate since early 2020, when it had to shut down boutiques globally due to the pandemic. Sales at Hermes' leather goods division, which makes its Birkin and Kelly handbags, climbed 10.8%, broadly in line with previous quarters. However, sales at the company's ready-to-wear and accessories division, accounting for over a quarter of quarterly sales, declined 2% from last year. Du Halgouet said the contraction was chiefly due to sluggish Chinese demand for high-volume accessories, while the division kept growing in all other regions. Ready-to-wear alone was up on the quarter, even when including China, he added. Accessories include items such as gloves, hair clips and belts – an important product category for Hermes because they often allow less wealthy shoppers make their first purchases with the brand. UPBEAT ABOUT US BUSINESS Chinese consumers, who account for roughly a fifth of global luxury purchases, were long the driving force behind the sector's growth, though demand has weakened sharply since the COVID pandemic. "As of the end of September, activity admittedly softened slightly in the third quarter, but it remains stable, which is still a significant feat in this very difficult market," du Halgouet said. The company remained optimistic about business in the United States, where it recently opened new stores in second-tier locations beyond the big coastal cities. All locations in the country and all product categories drove growth, du Halgouet said. Asked about [USN:S8N3Z600A TEXT:"recent unrest and violence"] in France, which led to the looting of one of its stores in the southern city of Marseille, Hermes said it would ramp up security measures. It was too early to call if the unrest would have a significant impact on its business, it said. Hermes shares are down 36% since the start of the year. Analysts have flagged a growing sense among investors that Hermes' historically high stock-market valuation, resulting from a decade of strong growth, may move closer to industry averages as the pace of its expansion is slowing. The brand's Birkin handbags have become more available on the second-hand market and so have lost some of their appeal, [USN:L6N46012F TEXT:"several resellers told Reuters"], suggesting Hermes' scarcity-driven business model could be coming under pressure. The Birkin's desirability remains "intact", du Halgouet said, adding the company would stick to its rhythm of increasing overall production volumes by around 6% in the coming years. ($1 = 0.8895 euros)

item.title: Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan GDP to contract 1.3% in 2026, IMF says
item.description: The IMF on Thursday forecast a sharp drop in economic output in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan this year due to the Iran war, followed by 6.6% growth in 2027, though it warned that further energy production disruptions could worsen the outlook.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Shalal, Federico Maccioni
item.content:encoded: The IMF on Thursday forecast a sharp drop in economic output in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan this year due to the Iran war, followed by 6.6% growth in 2027, though it warned that further energy production disruptions could worsen the outlook. The International Monetary Fund said the region's output was expected to contract by 1.3% as a result of the war's impact on energy production, shipping, tourism, trade and confidence. Economic growth would increase sharply in 2027, but output in those economies would generally stay below pre-war projections. The impact of the US-Israeli-led war against Iran had been substantial, but uneven, with oil-exporting economies directly affected by disruptions to energy production and shipping hit harder, and oil importers proving to be more resilient, the IMF said in its regional outlook released on Thursday in Dubai. "This sharp downgrade is concentrated among the economies most directly affected by the conflict," Jihad Azour, the IMF's director for the Middle East and Central Asia, said at a press conference. "Several Gulf oil exporters are projected to experience recession this year," he added. OUTLOOK CLOUDED BY 'HIGH UNCERTAINTY' According to the IMF regional outlook, Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economies are expected to contract in 2026, with Oman the exception. Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, along with non-GCC member Iraq, are forecast to post double-digit declines in gross domestic product. "Although relatively less affected by the disruptions in energy trade, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are now also projected to experience a recession in 2026," the IMF said in the report. It said its baseline assumed that the conflict would abate in early 2027 and that trade would gradually normalize during the year, but it said the outlook remained clouded by "exceptionally high uncertainty." "A more prolonged conflict remains the principal risk to the outlook," Azour said. The US State Department on Wednesday [USN:L6N46718Z TEXT:"ordered "]some diplomats and family members to leave its missions in Saudi Arabia and plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region, officials told Reuters. The move follows escalating missile strikes by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on the kingdom. External financial conditions could also tighten if investors reassess AI-driven productivity gains and interest rates rise further amid heightened concerns about inflation and fiscal positions, the IMF said in its outlook. Domestic demand in oil-importing economies is supported by remittances and tourism flows, favorable financial conditions, and prompt policy responses that safeguard consumers from higher commodity prices, the IMF said. Growth in the Caucasus and Central Asia was moderating toward a more sustainable pace, the IMF said, forecasting a 5.2% rise in economic output in 2026 and 5% in 2027. The IMF underscored the mantra it delivered during last week's annual meetings, urging policymakers to prioritize maintaining price stability, while preserving fiscal sustainability, maintaining central bank independence and enacting structural reforms to boost productivity and create jobs.

item.title: Surging sterling shakes off Britain's budget blues
item.description: Sterling is roaring into next week's UK budget, marking a dramatic change in mood from last year's trepidation and emerging as an eye-catching performer in otherwise nervy global markets.
item.dc:creator: Mike Dolan
item.content:encoded: Sterling is roaring into next week's [USN:L8N45R104 TEXT:"UK budget"], marking a dramatic change in mood from last year's trepidation and emerging as an [USN:L6N4650O5 TEXT:"eye-catching performer"] in otherwise nervy global markets. A change of political leadership in the interim may be the obvious difference from 2025. But a world more anxious about sovereign debt and tech-sector bubbles may now view Britain as a way to sidestep the worst of potential fallout. Shifts in relative interest rate horizons provide the simplest explanation for sterling strength, which is now probing 18-month highs against the euro and its best levels against the dollar in over four weeks. Surprisingly brisk UK growth, employment and inflation mean another [USN:L6N4600XN TEXT:"quarter-point rate hike"] has been added to the market's one-year Bank of England outlook over the past month, just as [USN:L6N46617I TEXT:"French debt tensions"] and the threat of euro zone contagion have lopped a quarter point off the European Central Bank view over the same period. The [USN:L6N46606V TEXT:"Federal Reserve's outlook"] is basically unchanged over the past month. But it's a punchy currency move nonetheless. Over the space of a month, sterling has risen almost 2.6% against a euro weighed down by French political angst and debt worries, but it also gained about 1% against a far more buoyant US dollar . While the premium on 10-year UK gilt yields over Germany has risen about 25 basis points in that time to nearly 2 percentage points, the gilt premium over French 10-year debt has halved to just 37 basis points. UK stock indexes (.FTSE) , (.FTMC) are up about 1%, too. Contrast that with former finance minister Rachel Reeves' final budget in late November last year, when fears over tax and borrowing plans had the pound, gilts and the FTSE equity benchmark all under pressure for weeks. Twelve months on, much has changed, not least the change of Labour prime minister in July, from Keir Starmer to Andy Burnham, and a change of finance minister from Reeves to John Healey. At the very least, the change at the top has transformed the government's opinion poll ratings - and that fact alone provides a major contrast to other European and US leaders. But most dramatically this year, the Iran war has shocked energy markets and upended inflation and interest-rate policy, potentially putting Britain back in the same boat it was in last year. Yet as [USN:L8N45R104 TEXT:"Healey prepares to unveil"] another difficult budget next week, struggling to keep spending within the government's own fiscal rules, he faces a very different market backdrop. Aided by a relatively tight fiscal stance, the BoE has so far held the line on interest rates this year despite hikes at the ECB and Fed. The economy has held up impressively and is one of the fastest-growing in the Group of Seven (G7) nations. It appears [USN:L6N46519A TEXT:"Healey is intent"] on not rocking that boat. MERCIFULLY BORING BUDGET? Deutsche Bank economist Sanjay Raja brands it the "Do no harm" budget, with limited tax and spending moves flagged in advance despite the narrow room Healey has to manoeuvre. Raja says the "low-key" affair will still matter for markets, with stability critical before much tougher government spending reviews next year. "A dull Budget need not be an unimportant budget," he wrote. Goldman Sachs senior UK economist James Moberly flagged higher borrowing projections given shifts in interest rates and gilt yields over the year, making it more important to avoid disturbing markets or the economy. And on that score, the[USN:L8N4661GS TEXT:" latest UK data sweep "]on Wednesday seemed jarring at first. British inflation and borrowing rose more than expected last month, with total government debt topping £3 trillion ($4 trillion) for the first time. The numbers also underlined why Britain looks relatively solid in a world of scarier sovereign debt metrics. Despite higher borrowing than official forecasts made before the Iran war, the [USN:L8N4661Q9 TEXT:"budget deficit for the first six months"] was more than £4 billion lower than last year, and the debt-to-GDP ratio is lower than 12 months ago, thanks to faster growth. At just over 100% of GDP, Britain's debt load and servicing costs are burdensome, but they are lower than those of France and the US. And while Germany's debt burden may still be lower, it's fast converging on British levels after a recent defence spending splurge. As ING's James Smith points out, Britain is one of the few major economies that's actually managing to rein in government finances at the moment, helping stay the BoE's hand. If growth is improving, then that starts to resonate. "Britain gets a bad rap on its public finances, but they're in better shape than many other developed economies right now," he said. "The UK is the only G7 economy currently doing fiscal consolidation." A long list of risky elections crowds the calendar over the coming year: US midterm elections, a snap election in Spain next month and French elections next April. Britain's more popular government and hefty majority may seem a calmer berth against all that. The only fly in that ointment is that Burnham sees the economic picture and polls as good enough to allow him to seek a popular mandate for his role in Number 10 Downing Street by calling a snap election next year. ING's Smith thinks that could upset markets again by introducing policy uncertainty, whether Labour wins or loses. That decision is likely to wait until 2027, however, and Healey's boring budget may just be what the doctor ordered in the meantime. Britain might actually look relatively good for a change. item.title: Don't mistake Mideast oil rebound for normality
item.description: Crude oil prices remain near five-month highs despite a recent surge in Middle East crude exports above pre-war levels and intensifying Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. This suggests investors may already be bracing for another round of regional escalation.
item.dc:creator: Ron Bousso
item.content:encoded: Crude oil prices remain near five-month highs despite a recent surge in Middle East crude exports [USN:L1N45R00B TEXT:"above pre-war levels"] and intensifying Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. This suggests investors may already be bracing for another round of regional escalation . The rebound in crude flows from the Gulf is striking. Middle East oil exports have averaged 17.3 million barrels per day (bpd) so far in October, up from 16.4 million bpd in September and above the 16.9 million bpd average in the two months before US-Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28, according to Kpler data. This reflects a surge in flows through the embattled Strait of Hormuz. Flows hit 11.7 million bpd in October, up from 9.75 million bpd in September. While still around 82% of pre-war levels, Hormuz flows are far above their wartime nadir of less than 1 million bpd in April, excluding Iranian oil, according to Kpler. The increase is largely thanks to the growing use of ship convoys that sail through the strait close to the Omani coastline under US naval protection. Shipping data suggests around a third of crossings continue to use the Iran-controlled northern route, most likely in coordination with Tehran, but those flows remain opaque. The sustained traffic is a clear sign that Gulf producers and tanker owners are willing to tolerate the risk of attack. Last week, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, an industry security advisory, reported 12 attacks in or around Hormuz, a record high. The agency said the actual number was probably much higher because many vessel owners do not report attacks, likely for commercial or security reasons. The broader recovery in regional exports has also been helped by the rapid rebound in Saudi shipments from the Red Sea port of Yanbu. An attack last month by Iran-backed Iraqi militias on a vital pipeline linking the kingdom's eastern oilfields with its western coast had crippled flows for weeks. [USN:L8N467118 TEXT:"Saudi Arabia’s"] Red Sea exports have averaged 3 million bpd so far in October. While below the wartime peak of 4.3 million bpd in June, that still represents a much faster-than-anticipated recovery. NEW ABNORMAL Higher flows should not be mistaken for a return to normality. Benchmark rates for a tanker carrying 2 million barrels of crude from the Middle East to China remain near an all-time high of around $1.4 million a day, more than 12 times pre-war levels. Tanker insurance costs have also risen to around 10% of the value of the cargo, up from roughly 3% before the war. Those extraordinary logistics costs are weighing heavily on refiners. Middle East producers have responded by [USN:L6N4620UK TEXT:"offering large discounts"] to offset those costs. In a bid to secure buyers for their oil, Saudi Aramco (2222.SE) and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co have also started selling some cargoes on a delivered basis to buyers in China and India, a sharp departure from the common practice of selling crude at the point of loading. Gulf producers are willing to risk sending tankers carrying cargoes worth more than $220 million through treacherous waters because securing export revenues and defending market share outweigh the mounting cost and danger of getting those barrels to customers. Producers and consumers have rapidly adapted to this “new abnormal,” creating a system that can deliver large volumes of crude, but only through an expensive and increasingly elaborate web of [USN:L6N45Q087 TEXT:"multi-ship transports"], military protection, heightened insurance fees, hefty discounts and altered sales terms. ADAPTATION ILLUSIONS On the surface, the adaptation appears to be working. The global volume of crude oil aboard tankers rose this week to around 157 million barrels on a four-week average, slightly above the level a year ago. Yet despite the recovery in physical supplies, benchmark Brent crude has climbed in recent days to around $110 a barrel, the highest price since May and not far off the wartime peak of $118 reached in March. The divergence between abundant barrels and rising prices suggests traders are concerned not about the amount of oil available today, but about whether Middle East exports can be sustained if – or, perhaps, when – fighting intensifies again. Meanwhile, daily trading volumes in ICE Brent options jumped on Tuesday to a record of more than 1 million lots, according to HiLo Analytics, another indication that producers and consumers, including refiners and airlines, are rushing to protect themselves against another violent swing in oil prices. Those concerns are growing ahead of [USN:L6N4670JK TEXT:"Israel's general election"] on October 27 and the US midterm elections one week later. President Donald Trump has said the US will not attack Iran before US polls, but he has sent additional warships to the region while threatening future attacks against Iranian nuclear facilities. Renewed [USN:S8N455017 TEXT:"diplomatic efforts"] involving Pakistani and Qatari mediators this week offer a path forward, but, if the signals coming from Tehran and Washington are any guide, they are unlikely to produce a breakthrough any time soon. The global energy system has proved far more resilient than seemed possible during the darkest days of the Iran war. Yet that adaptability comes at a cost, and producers, consumers and investors appear to believe it may keep rising. (The opinions expressed here are those of Ron Bousso , a columnist for Reuters.) item.title: Retail investors fully subscribe Ambani's Jio IPO on second day
item.description: Appetite for the $3.2 billion IPO of billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Jio Platforms kept building on Thursday, its second day of public bidding, with orders for shares more than four times the amount available and the retail portion fully subscribed.
item.dc:creator: Vibhuti Sharma
item.content:encoded: Appetite for the $3.2 billion IPO of billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Jio Platforms (JIOP.NS) kept building on Thursday, its second day of public bidding, with orders for shares more than four times the amount available and the retail portion fully subscribed. In what is set to be India's [USN:L6N467074 TEXT:"largest"] IPO and the first by Reliance in 20 years, the listing is a key plank of Ambani’s long-term vision to turn Reliance Industries (RELI.NS) from an oil-and-chemicals giant into an "everything company" spanning consumer, retail and technology. [USN:L1N467028 TEXT:"Institutional"] investors have led demand, with qualified institutional buyers bidding for 9.78 times their quota, exchange data showed. Retail investors, for whom around a third of the issue is reserved, covered their own portion in full by the first two hours in the second of three days of public bidding and had bid 1.29 times their quota. The IPO has generated strong retail demand in the primary market thanks largely to the Reliance brand, with a reach well beyond [USN:L1N46702L TEXT:"Jio Platforms"]' telecoms business, said an analyst tracking the IPO. For many Indian families, shareholdings in Reliance have long been a trusted nest egg, with its Mumbai-traded shares rising around 330-fold since 1990. Announcing the listing in June, Ambani described it as "a deeply emotional moment for me, for the entire Reliance Family, and millions of its shareholders." Jio helped put streaming, digital payments and online services within reach of millions of Indians through cheap data and free calls. Its next phase leans on 5G, home broadband and cloud and AI services. On its [USN:L1N467028 TEXT:"first"] day of public bidding, the overall offering was filled within 90 minutes of opening, driven by institutions that snapped up their portion within minutes. It was a rare start for an IPO of this size in India, where large offerings tend to see most bids in the final hours. The IPO has been watched as a barometer of global demand for new listings, with AI-linked companies facing tougher scrutiny. About 90% of Jio's revenue comes from its telecoms business. The IPO values Jio Platforms at up to $108.3 billion, potentially making it one of India's biggest companies by market capitalisation when trading starts on October 28. Jio's telecoms arm, led by Mukesh Ambani's son Akash, was built on a gamble in 2016: that cheap data would make Indians spend far more time online. Low prices and free voice calls drew subscribers away from Bharti Airtel (BRTI.NS) and Vodafone Idea (VODA.NS) in short order. Today, more than 500 million Indians subscribe to Jio, which houses the country's biggest telecoms operator and ranks behind only China Mobile (600941.SS) among carriers serving a single country.
